question: A young squire pulled a sword from an anvil set in a stone in a London churchyard. No knight in Britain could move the blade. The boy was named the true king. What was his name?
context: The sword in the stone was set there by Merlin. Letters of gold around it read 'Whoso pulleth out this sword from this stone is rightwise king born of all England.' Arthur drew it on the morning of a tournament, fetching it for his foster-brother Sir Kay.

question: Merlin took the infant Arthur in secret and gave him to a kind knight to be raised in the country, away from court. The knight raised Arthur as a foster son with his own boy Kay. Who was the knight?
context: Sir Ector did not know that the child Merlin gave him was Uther Pendragon's true heir. When Arthur drew the sword from the stone, Sir Ector and Kay both knelt to him. Kay later served as Arthur's seneschal at Camelot.

question: The high king of Britain before Arthur was a fierce warrior whose dragon banner gave him his second name. He was Arthur's true father. Who was he?
context: Pendragon means 'chief dragon' or 'head dragon' in old Welsh. Uther loved Igraine, the wife of Duke Gorlois, and Merlin disguised him as Gorlois so he could come to her. Arthur was conceived that night and given to Merlin to hide.

question: An arm in white silk rose from a misty lake holding a sword aloft. King Arthur rowed out and the Lady of the Lake gave him the enchanted blade. What was the sword called?
context: Excalibur's scabbard could protect its bearer from losing any blood from any wound — a gift even greater than the blade itself. Morgan le Fay later stole the scabbard, leaving Arthur defenseless against his fatal wound at Camlann.

question: A water-goddess in white silk lived in a lake hidden in the British forests. She gave King Arthur his sword Excalibur and later raised the orphan Lancelot in her underwater hall. What was she called?
context: Lancelot's surname 'du Lac' (of the Lake) comes from being fostered by her — she raised him after his royal parents lost their kingdom. In some retellings the Lady of the Lake and the wizard's prison-keeper Nimue are different women; in others, the same.

question: The wizard who hid the sword in the stone, raised Arthur in secret, and built the Round Table at Camelot saw the future and the past at once. What was the wizard's name?
context: Merlin was said to be the son of a mortal woman and an incubus. He prophesied the rise and fall of kings. He set the sword in the stone and prepared the Round Table at Camelot before falling under the spell of the damsel Nimue.

question: The aged wizard Merlin fell in love with a young enchantress. She wheedled all his magic out of him and then sealed him forever inside a hollow oak. What was her name?
context: Nimue (sometimes Vivienne or Viviane) was one of the maidens of the Lady of the Lake. Merlin knew her trick was coming but loved her too much to refuse her. In some versions she becomes the new Lady of the Lake after.

question: King Arthur's hall at Camelot held a single great table where no knight sat above any other — the very shape declared all equals around the king. What was the table called?
context: Merlin made the table for Uther Pendragon, who passed it to King Leodegrance, whose daughter Guinevere brought it back to Camelot as her dowry when she married Arthur. The table seated up to a hundred and fifty knights.

question: King Arthur's chief castle and royal seat was a city of high white towers, banners, and tournament fields where the knights of the Round Table feasted and rode out on quests. What was its name?
context: Different medieval writers placed Camelot at Caerleon in Wales, Cadbury Hill in Somerset, or Winchester in Hampshire. The name appears first in the French romances of Chretien de Troyes in the 12th century.

question: King Arthur's queen was the most beautiful woman in Britain, daughter of King Leodegrance of Cameliard. She brought the Round Table to Camelot as her dowry but loved another knight in secret. What was her name?
context: Guinevere's secret love was Sir Lancelot, the greatest knight of the Round Table. The discovery of their affair drove Lancelot from Camelot and gave Mordred the opening to seize Arthur's throne. After Arthur's death she became a nun at Amesbury.

question: The greatest knight of the Round Table was raised by the Lady of the Lake (which gave him his surname). He could not be beaten in single combat but loved Queen Guinevere. Who was he?
context: Lancelot 'du Lac' means 'of the Lake.' He arrived at Camelot a young knight and quickly became the king's champion. His son Galahad would be the one who finally achieved the Holy Grail. His secret love for Guinevere ended Arthur's reign.

question: King Arthur's nephew was one of the strongest knights of the Round Table — strongest of all between sunrise and noon, his strength growing with the sun. Who was he?
context: Gawain was the son of King Lot and Queen Morgause (Arthur's half-sister). He is best known from the 14th-century poem 'Sir Gawain and the Green Knight,' where he accepts a beheading game on Christmas at Camelot.

question: A naive knight raised by his mother in a forest, knowing nothing of chivalry, blundered into Arthur's court in country clothes — yet became one of the three who saw the Holy Grail. What was his name?
context: Percival's mother had hidden him from chivalry because her husband and sons had died as knights. He first appears in Chretien de Troyes's 'Perceval, le Conte du Graal' (c. 1180), the earliest Grail story. His Welsh original is Peredur.

question: Sir Lancelot's son was the purest knight ever to ride to Camelot. He alone could sit in the empty seat Merlin had reserved for the one worthy of the Holy Grail. What was his name?
context: Galahad's mother was Elaine of Corbenic. The empty seat at the Round Table was called the Siege Perilous — any unworthy knight sitting there would be destroyed. Galahad sat in it on his arrival and a vision of the Grail appeared in the hall.

question: A Cornish knight famous for his harp and his hunting horns drank a love potion meant for someone else and fell in love with Iseult, the Irish bride of his uncle King Mark. Who was he?
context: Tristan (Tristram in Malory) was sent to Ireland to bring back Princess Iseult for his uncle. On the ship home they drank the love potion her mother had prepared for King Mark. Their tragic story is one of the great medieval romances.

question: An Irish princess was sent across the sea to marry King Mark of Cornwall. On the voyage she and her escort Sir Tristan accidentally drank a love potion meant for the wedding night. What was her name?
context: Iseult (Isolde in some retellings) was the daughter of the Queen of Ireland. The love potion bound her and Tristan forever; the wedding to King Mark could never erase it. Their story inspired Richard Wagner's opera 'Tristan und Isolde' (1865).

question: One of only three knights to achieve the Holy Grail was the only one who returned alive to tell the tale at Camelot. He was Sir Lancelot's cousin. What was his name?
context: Galahad died in the vision of the Grail at Sarras; Percival died not long after; Bors alone rode home. Bors was famous for his strict chastity, second only to Galahad's, and once chose to let his brother be killed rather than save him by abandoning a damsel in distress.

question: Arthur's foster brother, the son of Sir Ector who raised him, served as Arthur's chief steward (seneschal) at Camelot. He was known for sharp wit and a sharper tongue. Who was he?
context: Sir Kay was raised alongside Arthur in Sir Ector's house. As a boy he sent young Arthur to fetch a sword from the churchyard during a tournament — and Arthur came back with the sword from the stone. Kay was rude but loyal; Arthur kept him close.

question: Arthur's last surviving knight at the battlefield of Camlann was a one-handed warrior who had been with him from the beginning. Arthur ordered him to throw Excalibur back into the lake. What was his name?
context: Bedivere twice hid Excalibur in the reeds and lied to the dying Arthur, claiming he had thrown it. Arthur knew he lied. The third time, Bedivere obeyed and an arm rose from the lake to catch the sword. Three queens then took Arthur to Avalon.

question: The traitor knight who seized King Arthur's throne while he was away was, in the later traditions, Arthur's own son by his half-sister. Who was he?
context: Mordred was the son of Arthur and Morgause (his half-sister), born from an unwitting union before Arthur knew their kinship. While Arthur was campaigning in France against Lancelot, Mordred seized the throne. They killed each other at the Battle of Camlann.

question: King Arthur's older half-sister was a powerful sorceress trained at the convent and by Merlin. She often plotted against Arthur — once stealing the scabbard of Excalibur. What was her name?
context: Morgan was the daughter of Igraine by her first husband, Duke Gorlois — making her Arthur's elder half-sister. 'Le Fay' means 'the fairy.' She is one of the three queens who carries Arthur to Avalon at the end. Sister, enemy, and final mourner all at once.

question: The knights of the Round Table rode out on a long, terrible quest for a single sacred cup — the one Christ had used at the Last Supper. What was the cup called?
context: In medieval legend, Joseph of Arimathea took the cup from the Last Supper, used it to catch blood at the Crucifixion, and carried it to Britain. The Grail quest tested every Knight of the Round Table; only Galahad, Percival, and Bors achieved it.

question: On Christmas at Camelot, a huge knight all in green rode in carrying an axe and proposed a beheading game — strike me once, and I strike you back in a year. Who took the challenge?
context: The Green Knight is the most famous of all Arthurian tales after Excalibur and the Grail. Gawain cut off the Green Knight's head — but the knight picked it up, reminded Gawain of the bargain, and rode out. Gawain spent the next year riding to keep his vow.

question: After being wounded at the battle of Camlann, the dying King Arthur was carried away in a black barge by three veiled queens to a mystical island of apple trees and healing. What was the island called?
context: The name Avalon comes from the old British word for 'apple.' Some traditions say Arthur died there; others say he sleeps still, healing of his wound, until Britain has need of him again. He is called 'rex quondam rexque futurus' — the once and future king.

question: An outlaw with a longbow lived in Sherwood Forest, robbing rich travelers to give to the poor. His best friend was a giant called Little John, and his band wore Lincoln green. Who was he?
context: The Robin Hood ballads first circulated in late-medieval England. His chief enemy was the Sheriff of Nottingham; his love was Maid Marian; his trusted advisor was Friar Tuck, a fighting monk. The earliest ballads date from the 14th century.

question: Robin Hood and his band of Merry Men hid from the Sheriff of Nottingham in a vast royal hunting forest in the English midlands. What was the forest called?
context: Sherwood Forest is a real woodland in Nottinghamshire, England — once a vast royal forest of oak. The Major Oak inside it is over 800 years old and traditionally pointed out as Robin's headquarters. King Henry II hunted there.

question: Robin Hood's band of outlaws wore a particular shade of woodland-camouflage cloth made in an English city famous for its dyers. The cloth was called what?
context: Lincoln green was a famous English woollen cloth dyed in the city of Lincoln using woad (blue) and weld (yellow). Outlaws hiding in Sherwood Forest wore it for camouflage among the leaves. The Merry Men's longbows could shoot a clothyard arrow over 300 yards.

question: Robin Hood met a giant of a man at a narrow log bridge over a forest stream. Neither would step aside. They fought with quarterstaffs and the giant knocked Robin into the water. What was the giant's name?
context: His real name was John Little — the nickname 'Little John' was a joke because he stood seven feet tall. After winning the fight he joined Robin's band as Robin's second-in-command. He was the band's best quarterstaff fighter.

question: One of Robin Hood's Merry Men was a hefty, ale-loving monk who fought as well with a sword and a quarterstaff as he prayed. He carried Robin across a river on his back. What was his name?
context: Friar Tuck was a corpulent fighting friar — a parish priest type rather than a strict-rule monk. In one famous ballad, Robin Hood asks Tuck to carry him across a river, then Tuck demands Robin carry him back, and they end up fighting in the water.

question: Robin Hood's true love was a noblewoman who fled to Sherwood Forest in disguise to join the outlaws. She fought as well as any of them with a quarterstaff. What was her name?
context: Maid Marian was added to the Robin Hood ballads in the 16th century from a French May-day pastoral. In the later legends she is a noblewoman, sometimes the ward of King Richard, who escapes a forced marriage by running to Sherwood and Robin.

question: Robin Hood's chief enemy was the corrupt king's officer in the city near Sherwood Forest. He raised heavy taxes for Prince John and chased Robin's band into the forest year after year. Who was he?
context: The Sheriff (literally 'shire-reeve') of Nottinghamshire was the king's chief officer in that county, responsible for collecting taxes and enforcing law. In the ballads the Sheriff tries to lure Robin into archery contests, fake amnesties, and dawn raids on the forest.

question: One of Robin Hood's Merry Men wore bright scarlet silk among the Lincoln green and was the band's finest swordsman. He was Robin's young cousin in some ballads. What was his name?
context: Will Scarlett (sometimes Scarlock or Scathelocke) was one of the oldest named Merry Men in the ballads, appearing in 'A Gest of Robyn Hode' (c. 1495). He was famous for the bright scarlet doublet he wore as a personal mark of pride.

question: The Sheriff of Nottingham held an archery contest as a trap. Robin Hood came in disguise and won. He hit the bullseye dead center, then loosed a second arrow that split his own first arrow in two. What did Robin win?
context: Splitting one's own previous arrow with the next is called a 'Robin Hood shot' in archery to this day. The Sheriff guessed too late which masked archer had won the prize. The Merry Men ambushed the road home and got Robin away.

question: Robin Hood and the Merry Men stopped rich travelers on the Sherwood Forest road, ate dinner with them, weighed their purses, and gave the silver away to a particular sort of person. To whom?
context: The phrase 'robbing the rich to give to the poor' became Robin Hood's defining motto. In the ballads he targets corrupt churchmen and the Sheriff's tax collectors specifically, sparing honest workmen, knights who have been wronged, and the poor altogether.

question: A Swiss hunter was ordered by an Austrian bailiff to shoot an apple off his own son's head with a single arrow at eighty paces — or be killed. He pulled it off cleanly. What was his name?
context: The bailiff was Hermann Gessler. Tell drew two arrows from his quiver — and after the shot, when Gessler asked why the second, Tell answered: 'If I had killed my son, the second arrow was for you.' He is the legendary founder of Swiss independence.

question: A Geatish hero sailed from Sweden with fourteen warriors to fight the monster terrorizing King Hrothgar's mead-hall in Denmark. He killed the beast bare-handed by tearing its arm off. What was the hero's name?
context: Beowulf is the hero of the oldest long poem in Old English (about 1,000 years old). The monster he killed was Grendel. He went on to kill Grendel's mother in her underwater lair and, fifty years later, died slaying a dragon in his own old age.

question: For twelve winters the great Danish mead-hall called Heorot was raided every night by a swamp-dwelling monster that devoured King Hrothgar's warriors. What was the monster's name?
context: Grendel was described in the poem as a descendant of Cain, walking the moors. He could not bear the sound of music and feasting from Heorot. Beowulf grappled with him bare-handed and tore his arm off at the shoulder; Grendel fled to die in his marsh.

question: Charlemagne's paladin Roland died holding two things at the pass of Roncevaux — his sword Durendal in one hand, and his ivory war-horn in the other. What was the horn called?
context: Olifant is from the same root as 'elephant' — it was carved from a tusk of ivory. Roland blew it three times so loudly the third blast burst the veins in his temples. Charlemagne heard it many miles away but arrived too late to save the rear-guard.

question: A Castilian knight named Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar was exiled by his king and rode out at the head of his own army to conquer the Mediterranean city of Valencia. By what title is he known?
context: 'El Cid' comes from the Arabic 'al-sayyid' meaning 'the lord.' He lived from about 1043 to 1099. His sword was named Tizona. The Spanish national epic 'Cantar de mio Cid' (c. 1200) tells his story; the 1961 film with Charlton Heston brought him back to wide notice.

question: A traveling musician in a patchwork coat offered to rid the German town of Hamelin of its rats. The town refused to pay. He returned and piped the children away into a hillside. What was he called?
context: 'Pied' means 'parti-colored' or 'patchwork.' The legend is set in 1284. A stained-glass window in Hamelin's old church recorded the disappearance of 130 children. Historians have tied the legend to a real medieval migration or to plague.

question: King Uther Pendragon loved Igraine, the wife of Duke Gorlois of Cornwall, and would not be turned away. The wizard Merlin took a strange payment in exchange for helping the king. He disguised Uther as Gorlois himself for a night at Tintagel castle. What did Merlin demand in return?
answer: The child born of that night, to be raised in secret
choices: The child born of that night, to be raised in secret
Half of Uther's kingdom upon his death
Uther's dragon banner and his crown jewels
Igraine herself as a captive once she was queen
context: The child was Arthur. The real Gorlois died that very night in battle elsewhere. Uther later married Igraine but kept his promise to Merlin: Arthur was given over to be hidden away in Sir Ector's house, raised as a foster son with Sir Kay.

question: A sword stood in an anvil set in a stone in a London churchyard. Letters around it read: 'Whoso pulleth out this sword from this stone is rightwise king born of all England.' Knights from across Britain tried to pull it free and could not. Then a young squire fetching a blade for his foster-brother lifted it cleanly. Who was the squire?
context: The sword in the stone was set by Merlin so the rightful heir to Uther Pendragon would be revealed. Arthur drew it on the morning of a tournament when his foster-brother Sir Kay had forgotten his sword. Kay tried to claim credit, then knelt to Arthur when Sir Ector pressed for the truth.

question: After Arthur broke his first sword (the one from the stone) in single combat against King Pellinore, Merlin took him to a misty lake. An arm rose from the water in white silk, holding aloft an enchanted blade. Arthur rowed out in a small boat and the Lady of the Lake gave him both the sword and its protective scabbard. What was the blade called?
context: In Malory's *Le Morte d'Arthur* (1485), Excalibur is distinct from the sword from the stone. Its scabbard prevented Arthur from losing blood from any wound. Morgan le Fay later stole the scabbard, leaving him fatally vulnerable to Mordred at Camlann.

question: When Arthur married Guinevere, her father King Leodegrance of Cameliard sent her dowry: an enormous round table with room for over a hundred knights, plus the knights who already sat at it. Merlin had originally made the table for Uther. Why was it built round?
answer: So no knight sat above any other in honor
choices: So no knight sat above any other in honor
To leave space for Merlin's enchantments in the center
To match the disk of the sun, sacred to Arthur
Because Camelot's old hall was a circular Roman ruin
context: The round shape declared all knights peers — Arthur sat among them, not above them. One seat called the Siege Perilous remained always empty, reserved by Merlin's prophecy for the knight pure enough to achieve the Holy Grail. Galahad was the only knight who could sit there safely.

question: The aged wizard Merlin foresaw that the young enchantress Nimue would one day trap him. He still followed her into the forest of Broceliande, teaching her every spell she asked. She finally sealed him forever inside a hollow oak. Why did he allow it, when he could see it coming?
answer: Because he loved her and could not refuse her
choices: Because he loved her and could not refuse her
Because prophecy demanded an heir to his magic
Because his life had run out and he hid to die
Because Arthur had ordered him into hiding
context: Nimue (also called Vivienne or Viviane) had been a damsel of the Lady of the Lake. In some versions she takes Merlin's place as the new Lady of the Lake. Even from his prison, Merlin's voice was sometimes heard giving counsel to passing knights. Tennyson retells the story in 'Idylls of the King.'

question: The greatest knight of the Round Table was Lancelot, raised by the Lady of the Lake in her underwater hall. He arrived young at Camelot, swore loyalty to Arthur, and quickly became the king's champion. But he secretly loved Arthur's queen, and she loved him in return. What was the queen's name?
context: The affair was the long secret of Camelot. When it was finally exposed by Sir Mordred and twelve knights ambushing them in the queen's chamber, Lancelot fled to France. Arthur pursued him with an army. Mordred used the king's absence to seize the throne, leading to the doomed final battle at Camlann.

question: On Christmas Day at Camelot, a huge knight all in green — green armor, green skin, green hair, green horse — rode into the hall carrying a battle-axe. He proposed a beheading game: any knight may strike him once with the axe, if that knight will receive an answering blow in a year and a day at the Green Chapel. Who took up the axe?
context: Gawain cut off the Green Knight's head with a single stroke. The huge stranger calmly picked up his own head, told Gawain to meet him in a year, and rode out. Gawain rode out the next winter to keep his vow. The 14th-century poem 'Sir Gawain and the Green Knight' is one of the masterpieces of Middle English.

question: King Mark of Cornwall sent his nephew Sir Tristan to bring back his bride, the Irish princess Iseult. Her mother had prepared a magical drink for Iseult and Mark to share on their wedding night to bind them in love forever. On the voyage home, Tristan and Iseult drank it by mistake. What did it do?
answer: Bound the two of them in love forever
choices: Bound the two of them in love forever
Gave Tristan a wound that would not heal
Made Iseult forget she ever knew Tristan
Killed any drinker but the true bridegroom
context: Tristan and Iseult could not love any other. King Mark married Iseult, but the lovers kept meeting in secret. Eventually Tristan was wounded by a poisoned blade and could only be healed by Iseult — but his jealous wife (also called Iseult, of the White Hands) lied about the color of the rescue ship's sail, and he died grieving. Iseult of Ireland arrived and died beside him.

question: Merlin had reserved one chair at the Round Table — the Siege Perilous — for the one knight pure enough to achieve the Holy Grail. Any unworthy knight who sat in it was destroyed. A young knight in white armor arrived at Camelot on the feast of Pentecost and sat down in the chair without harm. Who was he?
context: Galahad was the son of Sir Lancelot and Elaine of Corbenic. That same evening, a vision of the Holy Grail appeared at the Round Table, veiled in white samite. Every knight present swore an oath to seek the Grail until it was found. The quest scattered the fellowship of Camelot.

question: King Arthur's knights rode out on a quest for a particular sacred cup. According to the medieval legend, this cup had been used by Christ at the Last Supper and later by Joseph of Arimathea to catch his blood at the Crucifixion. Only three knights ever achieved it. What was it called?
context: The Grail tradition appears in Chretien de Troyes (12th c.) and is fully developed in the *Queste del Saint Graal* (13th c.). The three knights who achieved the Grail were Galahad, Percival, and Bors. Galahad died in the vision at Sarras; Percival died not long after; Bors alone returned to Camelot.

question: A widow in a forest hid her young son from chivalry because her husband and elder sons had all died as knights. The boy grew up in country clothes, knowing nothing of swords. One day he saw five armored riders pass through the woods, thought they were angels, and ran to Camelot to become a knight himself. What was the boy's name?
context: Percival's story is the heart of Chretien de Troyes's 'Perceval, le Conte du Graal' (c. 1180), the first Grail romance. He arrived at Camelot still in his peasant clothes, blundering through court manners — yet became one of three knights to achieve the Grail. His Welsh original is the hero Peredur.

question: On the Grail quest Sir Bors came across a fork in the road. To the left, his brother Lionel was being beaten by two knights. To the right, a damsel was being carried off to be ravished by another knight. He could save only one. Which did he choose?
answer: The damsel he did not know
choices: The damsel he did not know
His brother Lionel from the two knights
Both, by sending a stranger he met to help his brother
Neither, withdrawing in prayer for guidance
context: Bors saved the damsel. Lionel survived but never forgave his brother. The story is in the *Queste del Saint Graal* (13th c.) and Malory's *Le Morte d'Arthur* — it makes Bors the second-purest knight after Galahad, since his choice put a stranger's honor above his own kin's life.

question: Excalibur's scabbard kept King Arthur from losing blood from any wound. As long as he wore it, no battle injury could kill him. His older half-sister, a powerful sorceress, stole the scabbard while he slept and threw it into a lake. Who took it?
context: Morgan was the daughter of Igraine by her first husband Duke Gorlois — Arthur's elder half-sister. Without the scabbard, Arthur could be wounded normally. At the battle of Camlann, Mordred's spear pierced the king's body — the scabbard could not save him then. Morgan was also one of the three queens who carried Arthur away to Avalon.

question: While Arthur was campaigning in France against Sir Lancelot, his nephew Mordred (in later traditions, Arthur's secret son) seized the throne. Arthur raced home. The armies met on Salisbury Plain. A truce was negotiated — then a soldier drew his sword to kill a snake by his foot. What followed?
answer: Both armies charged and slaughtered each other
choices: Both armies charged and slaughtered each other
Mordred fled the field on a fresh white horse
Lancelot arrived in time and routed the rebels
Merlin appeared and froze both sides in place
context: Arthur killed Mordred with his spear at Camlann, but with his final strength Mordred drove his own blade through Arthur's helmet into his skull. The battle was a catastrophe — almost every Round Table knight died. Sir Bedivere was Arthur's last surviving companion.

question: Dying after the battle of Camlann, King Arthur ordered his last knight, Sir Bedivere, to take Excalibur to a nearby lake and throw it in. Bedivere twice hid the sword in the reeds and lied to Arthur, claiming he had thrown it. Arthur knew he lied. What did Bedivere finally see when he obeyed the third time?
answer: An arm rose from the lake and caught the sword
choices: An arm rose from the lake and caught the sword
The water boiled and the sword sank like a stone
A great fish leapt up and swallowed the blade
The lake froze around the spot Excalibur fell
context: The arm that took back Excalibur was the Lady of the Lake's — the same hand that had given it to Arthur years before. After the sword was returned, three queens (including Morgan le Fay) arrived in a black barge to carry the dying Arthur away across the water to Avalon.

question: After the affair with Queen Guinevere drove the kingdom into civil war and Arthur died at Camlann, Sir Lancelot returned from France to find the queen had become a nun at Amesbury Abbey. They met one last time and parted forever. What did Lancelot do afterward?
answer: Became a hermit-priest and died of grief
choices: Became a hermit-priest and died of grief
Sailed back to France to be a great lord
Killed Mordred's surviving sons in revenge
Took ship for the Holy Land to die a Crusader
context: Lancelot took holy orders at a small hermitage and lived as a priest for the rest of his days. Guinevere died as a nun shortly before him. He buried her beside Arthur at Glastonbury. The story is the final book of Malory's *Le Morte d'Arthur* (1485).

question: As King Arthur lay dying after Camlann, a black barge came across the water carrying three veiled queens. They took him aboard and bore him away to the apple-isle of Avalon to heal his wounds. One of the three was his old enemy. Who was it?
choices: Nimue the Lady of the Lake
context: Morgan was Arthur's elder half-sister — enemy in life, mourner in death. In Geoffrey of Monmouth's 12th-century 'Life of Merlin,' Morgan rules Avalon as a healer-queen. The two other queens are variously named the Queen of Northgalis and the Queen of the Wastelands.

question: King Arthur did not exactly die at the end. The legends say he was carried to the island of Avalon to be healed of his wound, and he sleeps there still — awaiting the hour Britain has need of him. What Latin title did medieval writers give him?
answer: Rex quondam rexque futurus (the once and future king)
choices: Rex quondam rexque futurus (the once and future king)
context: T. H. White borrowed the phrase for his 1958 novel 'The Once and Future King,' the basis of the musical 'Camelot.' Sleeping-king legends are also attached to Charlemagne in Germany, Frederick Barbarossa, Holger Danske of Denmark, and Constantine XI Palaiologos in Greek tradition.

question: Sir Lancelot was tricked into spending the night with Princess Elaine of Corbenic when she was enchanted to appear to him as Queen Guinevere. Their son grew up to be the purest knight of the Round Table — the only one to fully achieve the Holy Grail. What was the son's name?
context: Galahad was raised in the convent until he was ready for knighthood. He arrived at Camelot on the Feast of Pentecost, sat in the Siege Perilous without harm, and rode out on the Grail quest. He died in the vision of the unveiled Grail at the holy city of Sarras.

question: A year after cutting off the Green Knight's head at Camelot, Sir Gawain rode to the Green Chapel for the return blow. He bent his neck under the giant axe. The Green Knight swung — feinting, stopping short, then nicking the skin. Why did the Green Knight spare him?
answer: Because Gawain had been almost wholly honest as a guest
choices: Because Gawain had been almost wholly honest as a guest
Because Gawain had outfought him in single combat first
Because the year-and-a-day vow ended at the first stroke
Because King Arthur rode in disguise to plead for his life
context: The Green Knight was actually Sir Bertilak, Gawain's host the previous nights. While Bertilak hunted, his wife had tested Gawain — Gawain had returned every kiss to his host as the bargain required, but kept one item (a magic green girdle promising protection). The nick on his neck punished the one kept thing.

question: Arthur's foster brother served as his chief steward (seneschal) at Camelot — keeping the household, the kitchens, the feasts, and the rules of the court. He was sharp-tongued and often rude to new knights, but he had grown up beside Arthur and was utterly loyal to him. What was his name?
context: Sir Kay was the son of Sir Ector, the knight Merlin had given the infant Arthur to raise. As a young man it was Kay's missing sword Arthur had run to fetch on tournament day — and Arthur came back with the sword from the stone. Kay first tried to claim the kingship for himself, then knelt to his foster-brother when their father pressed for the truth.

question: When Queen Guinevere was kidnapped by the knight Meleagant, Sir Lancelot pursued on foot after his horse was killed. A peasant offered him a ride in a low cart — a vehicle used for carrying criminals to the gallows. Lancelot hesitated two steps before climbing in. What did the two-step pause cost him?
answer: Guinevere's anger for valuing honor over her rescue
choices: Guinevere's anger for valuing honor over her rescue
His knighthood, taken by Arthur's royal order
The right to wear his shield at any tournament
Three years of pilgrimage for the disgrace done
context: The story is in Chretien de Troyes's 'Le Chevalier de la Charrette' (c. 1180), the earliest French Lancelot romance. Even hesitating two steps before sacrificing his reputation made Lancelot's love less than perfect in her eyes. He fought Meleagant, rescued her, and the story is the first to name the Lancelot-Guinevere affair.

question: In some retellings, young Arthur was nicknamed 'the Wart' by his foster-brother Kay because his real name had been kept secret by Merlin. T. H. White's 'The Sword in the Stone' (1938) follows this version. What unusual education did Merlin give the boy?
answer: Turned him into different animals to learn their wisdom
choices: Turned him into different animals to learn their wisdom
Made him memorize every law and chronicle of Britain
Trained him at swordplay until his hands bled raw
Hid him in a monastery to learn Latin and theology
context: T. H. White's 'The Once and Future King' begins with 'The Sword in the Stone.' Merlin turns young Arthur into a fish, a hawk, an ant, a wild goose, and a badger so he can learn how different creatures see the world. Disney adapted it as the 1963 animated film of the same name.

question: Medieval legend traced the Holy Grail back to a particular cup used at a particular meal in Jerusalem. After the meal, Joseph of Arimathea took it, used it to catch blood at the cross, and (according to British tradition) carried it across the sea to Glastonbury. At what meal was it first used?
choices: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
The Passover meal of King Herod
context: The Grail tradition was first set down by Chretien de Troyes (12th c.) and developed by Robert de Boron, who explicitly named it as the cup of the Last Supper. Glastonbury Abbey claimed Joseph of Arimathea founded the first British church there, planting his pilgrim's staff which grew into the Glastonbury Thorn.

question: Robin Hood came to a narrow log bridge over a forest stream and met a giant of a man coming the other way. Neither would step aside. They cut quarterstaffs from the nearest oak and fought on the slippery log until one knocked the other into the cold water. Who got dunked?
context: The giant was John Little — the Merry Men later joke-renamed him 'Little John' because he stood seven feet tall. After winning the staff-fight, John joined Robin's band on the spot. He became Robin's chief lieutenant and the band's best quarterstaff fighter.

question: The Sheriff of Nottingham held an archery contest to lure Robin Hood out of hiding. Robin came in disguise as a beggar with a patched eye. He won by shooting a perfect bullseye, then loosing a second arrow that split the first one straight down the middle. What did the Sheriff award him?
choices: A purse of one hundred marks
context: Splitting one's own previous arrow with a second shot is called a 'Robin Hood' in archery to this day. The Sheriff only realized which archer had won by reading a note tied to an arrow that Robin shot into the sheriff's hall window after the merry men had escaped Sherwood with the prize.

question: Robin Hood needed to cross a river and asked a heavy, ale-loving monk fishing on the bank to carry him over on his back. The monk carried him across. Then the monk drew his sword and ordered Robin to carry him back across. Then Robin demanded a third trip. What happened in the middle of the third crossing?
answer: The friar dropped Robin in the middle of the river
choices: The friar dropped Robin in the middle of the river
Robin laughed and gave the friar a gold coin
Little John ambushed them from the trees
The Sheriff's men arrived and arrested both
context: The friar was Friar Tuck, who joined the Merry Men after the fight. He carried both a sword and a quarterstaff under his robe and was as quick to fight as to bless. The river-crossing ballad is one of the oldest Robin Hood tales, dating to about the 15th century.

question: An abbot riding through Sherwood Forest was stopped, fed, and asked to pay for the meal. The Merry Men ate well with the stranger before weighing his purse. Then the abbot threw off his disguise — and revealed himself as a man so famous Robin Hood fell to his knees. Who was he?
context: King Richard I (the Lionheart, 1157-1199) had returned from the Third Crusade and his Austrian imprisonment to find his brother John misruling England. He pardoned Robin and the band, and according to some ballads gave Robin a knighthood and lands. After Richard's death in 1199, John reissued the outlawry and Robin returned to Sherwood.

question: Robin Hood's true love was a noblewoman who fled a forced marriage to ride to Sherwood Forest in male disguise as a page. She fought Robin himself with a sword in the forest, neither recognizing the other, until they paused exhausted. Who was she?
context: Maid Marian was added to the Robin Hood tradition in the 16th century, originally from the May Games. In later legends she is a noblewoman, often a ward of King Richard, escaping a marriage Prince John has arranged. She becomes one of the Merry Men's deadliest fighters, second only to Little John with the quarterstaff.

question: One of the oldest of Robin Hood's Merry Men is named in the 1495 ballad 'A Gest of Robyn Hode.' He wore not the Lincoln green of the rest of the band but a bright scarlet doublet, as his personal mark of pride. He was the band's finest swordsman. What was he called?
context: Will Scarlett (also Scarlock or Scathelocke in the earliest ballads) is often described as Robin's young cousin. In the 1976 film 'Robin and Marian' he is played in tragic old age. The bright scarlet against the green forest made him a hard target for the Sheriff's men to track.

question: One of Robin Hood's oldest named companions was the son of a miller from a nearby village. He was small, quick, fierce, and one of the original three or four Merry Men. He appears in the earliest 15th-century ballads. What was his name?
context: Much the Miller's Son appears in the late-medieval ballad 'Robin Hood and the Monk' alongside Little John, and in 'A Gest of Robyn Hode' (c. 1495). His name 'Much' was either a personal name or a play on his small size. He was Robin's lookout and a deadly bowman in his own right.

question: Robin Hood was bled to death (in some ballads, deliberately bled too far) by a treacherous prioress at Kirklees Priory in Yorkshire. Dying, he asked Little John for one last thing. He raised a bow, shot one arrow out the window, and asked to be buried where it fell. What did Little John bring him?
answer: His bow and a single arrow
choices: His bow and a single arrow
A silver hunting horn to blow
His old quarterstaff to lean on
context: Robin Hood's death is told in 'A Gest of Robyn Hode' (c. 1495) and 'Robin Hood's Death' (17th c.). A stone marked Robin Hood's Grave was raised at Kirklees Priory in Yorkshire and was already a tourist site in the 17th century. The prioress was said to be his own cousin.

question: A young minstrel met Robin Hood weeping on the forest road because his bride was being forced to marry a rich old knight. Robin disguised himself as a harper, walked into the church, and stopped the wedding. Who took the bride home as his wife in the end?
choices: Robin Hood himself, as her champion
Little John, who fell in love at sight
Friar Tuck, who married her by accident
context: Allan a Dale (sometimes Alan-a-Dale) was Robin's minstrel-companion in the later ballads. Friar Tuck (or in some versions a real priest, hurried in) performed the new ceremony at sword-point. Allan a Dale appears in 17th-century broadside ballads and was made famous again in Walter Scott's 'Ivanhoe' (1819).

question: The Merry Men stopped a heavy wagon on the king's road through Sherwood. The driver showed his Sheriff's seal and demanded passage. The Merry Men politely ignored him and weighed every chest. Whose money was the Sheriff transporting toward London in the wagon?
answer: King John's tax revenue from Nottinghamshire
choices: King John's tax revenue from Nottinghamshire
Cathedral tithes for the Bishop of York
The dowry of the Sheriff's own daughter
Mercenary pay for the Welsh border garrisons
context: The historical Prince John (later King John) ran England with a heavy hand during Richard's Crusade-and-imprisonment absence (roughly 1190-94). The Robin Hood ballads weave their stories into that resentment. Robin's targets in the ballads are specifically corrupt churchmen, royal tax officers, and grasping nobles — never honest workmen or wronged knights.

question: The Habsburg bailiff Hermann Gessler hung his hat on a pole in Altdorf, Switzerland, and decreed everyone passing must bow to it. A hunter walking through with his small son Walter refused. Gessler ordered the hunter shot — unless he could shoot an apple off his son's head from eighty paces. Who was the hunter?
context: Tell took two arrows from his quiver before the shot. He split the apple cleanly. When Gessler asked why the second arrow, Tell answered: 'If I had killed my son, the second arrow was for you.' He is the legendary founder of Swiss independence; Friedrich Schiller dramatized the story in his 1804 play 'Wilhelm Tell.'

question: The Geatish hero Beowulf sailed from Sweden with fourteen warriors to help King Hrothgar of the Danes. For twelve winters the king's great mead-hall Heorot had been raided by a swamp-monster every night. Beowulf chose to fight the monster bare-handed. What was the monster's name?
context: Beowulf grappled with Grendel in the dark hall and tore his arm off at the shoulder. Grendel fled to die in his marsh. The arm was nailed up as a trophy in Heorot. The next night Grendel's mother came for revenge — Beowulf had to dive into her underwater lair to kill her too, with a giant's sword found on her wall.

question: In 778 AD, the rear-guard of Charlemagne's army was ambushed by Basque mountain warriors in the narrow pass of Roncevaux in the Pyrenees. The paladin commanding the rear-guard carried an ivory war-horn that could summon Charlemagne's main army back. He refused to blow it until almost every man was dead — too proud. Who was he?
context: Roland's horn was named Olifant (from the same root as 'elephant,' since it was carved of ivory). When he finally blew it three times, the third blast burst the veins in his temples. *The Song of Roland* (c. 1100), the oldest major French poem, tells the story. His sword was named Durendal; his betrayer was his stepfather Ganelon.

question: The Castilian knight Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar was exiled by King Alfonso VI of Castile around 1081 and rode out to make his own kingdom — fighting both Christian and Muslim lords as the work came. By 1094 he had conquered the great Mediterranean port of Valencia. By what title was he known?
context: 'El Cid' comes from the Arabic 'al-sayyid' meaning 'lord' — used respectfully by both Christian and Muslim soldiers under his command. His sword was named Tizona, his horse Babieca. The Spanish national epic 'Cantar de mio Cid' (c. 1200) is the oldest preserved Castilian epic poem.

question: A traveling musician in a coat of many colors offered to rid the German town of Hamelin of its rats for a fee. He played his pipe and led every rat into the river to drown. The town refused to pay him. He returned, played a different tune, and led 130 children away into a hillside that closed behind them. In what year was this said to happen?
context: The disappearance was recorded on a stained-glass window in the old church of Hamelin (in Lower Saxony, Germany). Historians have tied the legend to a real medieval migration of young townspeople, or to the bubonic plague reaching the area. The Brothers Grimm collected the story; Robert Browning wrote the famous English poem 'The Pied Piper of Hamelin' (1842).

question: After William the Conqueror won the Battle of Hastings in 1066, a Saxon thane led a guerrilla resistance from the marshes and reedy islands of the fens around the Isle of Ely. He raided Norman camps and held out for years. What was he called?
context: 'Wake' means 'watchful' in Old English. Hereward raided the Norman-held abbey at Peterborough in 1070 and held the Isle of Ely against William's army for over a year, until the monks finally betrayed his path through the fens. The legend gave Charles Kingsley's 1865 novel 'Hereward the Wake' its hero.
